categories.summary: Wings, control surfaces and fins push along their surface normal once airspeed passes 15 m/s, with force proportional to rudder_surface_area (wings 8 to 120, control surfaces 10 to 70, fins 2 to 12). Control surfaces deflect about 45° each way, fins about 14.3°.

sections.title: Sizing
sections.body: rudder_surface_area: wings 8, 20, 40, 70, 120; control surfaces 10, 28, 70; control fins 2, 8, 12. The air force is proportional to this field, so at the same airflow, body mass and altitude the large control surface pushes 7 times as hard as the small one. The listed voxel count does not enter the equation.

sections.title: Deflection
sections.body: The game turns the input into an angle in radians. Control surfaces store 0.785398, about 45° each way, and fins 0.25, about 14.3°, so a fin is the finer, smaller-authority choice. Each update the surface moves toward the requested position. With full electrical supply it gets there in one update; a weak supply slows it, and no supply holds it.

sections.title: Stabilisers
sections.body: Reaction wheels carry force fields 10, 100 and 1000, a factor of ten per size; wire them to an aligned angular speed sensor.

sections.title: Air force
sections.body:
Wings, control surfaces and fins share one air routine. It pushes along the surface normal with force 24 × rudder_surface_area × P × B × (1 - immersion) × (airspeed - 15) × (normal airspeed + wing term). Airspeed is the surface's speed relative to the wind in m/s, and at 15 m/s or less there is no air force. P = (1 - 2.2413793e-05 × height)^5.3595023 is the altitude pressure ratio, 1 at sea level and 0 above 40000 m. B = min(0.00003 × body mass, 0.2), so the coefficient stops growing at a body mass of 6666.67.

Wing sections (rudder_type 1) add a wing term 3 × c^5 × g. c is the cosine between the direction of travel through the air and the wing's forward axis, the reverse of its dynamic_rotation_axes vector, and g rises from 0 at 15 m/s to 1 at 40 m/s. Travelling along that axis, the term lifts a wing even at zero angle of attack; travelling the other way removes it. Matching that axis to a visible mesh edge is an inference. Control surfaces and fins (rudder_type 0) have no wing term, so they push only when the air meets them at an angle.

The routine multiplies by its own constant 24 and does not read the shipped lift_force setting (0.25), so changing lift_force does not change this force.

sections.title: Lift and drag
sections.body:
The force is a single push along the normal. With angle of attack α between the airflow and the surface, lift is that force × cos α and drag is force × sin α. Plane resistance grows with airspeed × (airspeed - 15); the wing term grows with (airspeed - 15) × g. There is no stall angle, Reynolds-number term or separate skin drag in this routine.

Example: a small wing section (area 8) on a body of mass 1000 at 30 m/s and 10° angle of attack gets a normal force of 594.2, of which 585.1 is lift and 103.2 is drag.

sections.title: Force units and limit
sections.body:
The result is in the game's internal force units. Body mass is not calibrated to kilograms, so do not read it as newtons. The game queues the force once per update and the physics solver integrates it, so it is not multiplied by 60. Before it is applied its size is limited to 5 × S, where S is a per-vehicle scale passed in by the component dispatcher; area scaling is linear only below that limit.

Partly under water, the air force is scaled by 1 minus the immersion fraction and a separate water term takes over.

limitations: The force equations come from static decompilation of one build; the game was not run. How the game builds the cap scale S for craft joined by locked joints was not decoded, so forces near the cap are not predicted.
Which visible edge and editor arrow match positive deflection and the sign of the force was not checked in game.
Internal mass and force units are not calibrated to kilograms and newtons.
Reaction wheels are outside the air-force decode; their force fields are configuration only.

categories.summary: Buttons accept an external on/off input so several buttons can drive one output; the large keypad also emits a pulse on confirm.

sections.title: Wiring
sections.body: Chain buttons through External Input to unify outputs. Toggle buttons and lock buttons can set their default state in the properties.

limitations: Tooltip semantics only.

categories.summary: Monitors and HUDs draw on a logical grid of 32 pixels per block across their X and Z voxel bounds, from 32×32 on a Monitor 1x1 to 288×160 on a Monitor 9x5. Touch Output returns the screen size and two touch points in pixels.

sections.title: Wiring
sections.body: Feed Video Signal from a microcontroller or camera, connect Electric and turn Power Switch on. For a touchscreen, wire Touch Output to a composite input on the microcontroller that draws the screen and its video output back to Video Signal. While the screen is switched off, every Touch Output channel reads 0.

sections.title: Resolution
sections.body:
The game sets width = 32 × (voxel_max.x - voxel_min.x + 1) and height = 32 × (voxel_max.z - voxel_min.z + 1) from the definition's block bounds. The same size comes back from screen.getWidth() and screen.getHeight() in onDraw and on Touch Output number channels 1 and 2.

Sizes in pixels: Monitor 1x1 32×32, Monitor 1x2 64×32, Monitor 1x3 96×32, Monitor 2x2 64×64, Monitor 2x3 96×64, Monitor 3x3 96×96, Monitor 5x3 160×96, Monitor 9x5 288×160, HUD Small 32×32, HUD Large 96×96.

The listed voxel count and monitor_border do not change the pixel grid. The graphics quality setting scales the render target by 1, 2 or 4 after the size is stored, so it leaves the Lua and touch grid alone.

sections.title: Touch Output
sections.body:
Touch Output is a composite. Number channels 1 and 2 carry the width and height in pixels, 3 and 4 the X and Y of the first touch, and 5 and 6 the X and Y of the second. Boolean channels 1 and 2 are on while the first and second touch are pressed. Coordinates are whole pixels from the upper left, X to the right and Y down, accepted from 0 up to the width and height inclusive.

The screen tracks at most two touches at once and ignores a third. Releasing a touch clears only its flag and leaves its last X and Y on the channels, so check the flag before using a coordinate. The touch area is the screen face inset by monitor_border on each side, stretched over the pixel grid.

sections.title: Lua callbacks
sections.body: Read the channels with input.getNumber and input.getBool in onTick, which runs once per logic tick; screen functions do nothing there. Draw in onDraw, which runs whenever a monitor draws the script and can run several times when one script drives several monitors. Composite functions do nothing in onDraw. The shipped example reads number channels 3 and 4 and boolean channel 1 in onTick and draws the matching rectangle in onDraw.

limitations: Resolution and touch layout come from static analysis of one build and its shipped definitions; the game was not run and no touch was tested in game.

Still open: a fixed refresh rate in Hz and the delay from a touch to the next drawn frame. onDraw follows monitor rendering rather than the 60-per-second component update, and the draw scheduling, culling and caching were outside this pass.
Still open: which player or input event takes each touch slot, and how HUD hits reach the touch setter.

categories.summary: Battery capacity is electric_charge_capacity (1 : 8 : 160 across sizes), and every full source lends at most 10 internal charge per update to the shared pool that consumers draw from. electric_magnitude is a per-component multiplier on charge: a motor pays electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1 per RPS of speed step, and a generator earns the same product per RPS it removes.

sections.title: Storage
sections.body:
The electric-node initialiser copies electric_charge_capacity straight into the node: 1600, 12800 and 256000 for the small, medium and large battery. A large battery stores 160 times a small one. Batteries also have a Charge Level property from 0 to 100 that sets the stored charge when the vehicle spawns.

Each update the game builds a temporary pool for every connected electric group, joining groups bridged by relays and breakers. Every battery, generator buffer, solar cell and charger lends a packet of min(C, 10) × b, where C is its capacity and b its stored fraction from 0 to 1. The pool's charge fraction q = E ÷ P is the lent charge E over the summed packet sizes P. Consumers then draw from E and generators add to it. At the end the remaining E goes back to each source in proportion to its packet, clamped to full, and the pool is discarded.

So every full battery lends the same 10 per update whatever its size, at most 600 per simulated second before generation. More batteries raise the charge available per update; a bigger battery only lasts longer. It follows that batteries on one network move toward the same fraction, small ones faster. Generation that would overfill the storage is lost.

sections.title: What electric_magnitude does
sections.body:
The field is read at definition+0x1420 by six instructions in this build, and the formula differs per component. In the electric component update, a motor (electric_type 0) asks the network for |Δ| × electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1, where Δ is the speed step in RPS it wants this update. A generator (electric_type 1) deposits electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1 × |ω| × min(|ω| ÷ 560, 0.25), where ω is the shaft speed in RPS. In both cases the speed change itself does not involve electric_magnitude. The field only sets how much charge a given speed change costs or earns, so for motors it works like an inverse efficiency (1.2, 1.1, 1.05) and for generators like an efficiency (0.6, 0.75, 0.85).

Generators get an internal buffer of 0.1 per listed voxel; solar cells and chargers get 0.01. No direct electric_magnitude read was found for batteries, breakers, relays, solar cells or chargers in this update; reads through differently computed pointers were not covered.

sections.title: Shaft speed
sections.body:
The motor and generator speed state is RPS: the save field is named rotations_per_second, the parts exchange it with the shaft unchanged, and a torque meter copies the same group speed to its RPS output. Each update a part submits its speed and its force_emitter_max_force as weight F to its shaft group. The group's new speed is (previous group speed + Σ F × submitted speed) ÷ (1 + Σ F), so the shaft itself carries weight 1, and each part takes that speed back.

Example: from rest, a part of weight 2 at 20 RPS and a part of weight 1 at 0 give (0 + 2 × 20 + 1 × 0) ÷ (1 + 2 + 1) = 10 RPS. A gearbox or clutch between two groups adds a weighted share of the other group's speed, reduced by the engagement and by 0.95 per link, with the ratio setting its sign and weight. The torque meter's Torque output reads the group's effective weight, not a torque in newton-metres.

sections.title: Other components that reuse the field
sections.body: The field is not a global efficiency. The classic diesel engines (field value 1.2) use it as a starter cost factor: max(5 − speed, 0) × engine_max_force × Max Power ÷ 2000 × electric_magnitude × 0.1. The modular starter (0.2) requests max(5 − crank speed, 0) × electric_magnitude × engine_max_force × 0.1. The modular alternator (0.05) uses the generator formula with an extra 0.1. The jet turbine branch (field value 0.025, investigation/jet-engines.md) deposits |ω| × electric_magnitude × min(ω ÷ 10000, 0.02) when that is positive, with no force term. The modular clutch, drive belt and temperature sensor carry values (1, 1, 0.05) that none of the six reads uses; the scan covers only direct +0x1420 operands.

sections.title: Supply and settings
sections.body:
Motors and both starters draw through the same helper. With infinite_batteries on it returns 1 and removes nothing. A part with no electric network gets 0. Otherwise, for a request R it removes T = min(a × R, E) from the pool and returns T ÷ R, where a = max(0, (300 − n) ÷ 300) × q. Here n is the part's EMP countdown and q the pool charge fraction. A motor's step is scaled by the returned fraction, so starving it slows acceleration without changing the cost per unit of step. Generators deposit regardless of infinite_batteries.

Low charge, an exhausted pool or consumers that drew first each cut supply on their own. q is fixed when the pool is built, so generation later in the same update raises E but not q until the next update. Which consumer draws first depends on the vehicle's component order.

An EMP pulse adds to n, and n counts down by 1 every update whether or not the part has power. At n = 300 or more the part gets nothing. Below 300 supply recovers linearly and is full again when n reaches 0, 300 updates (5 simulated seconds) later. A pulse also switches circuit breakers off. Inspecting an electric port shows max(0, 1 − n ÷ 300) × q as a bare number, or 1 with infinite electricity.

sections.title: Rates and units
sections.body: Component updates run 60 times per simulated second, so 60 × the charge per update is the charge per simulated second, in internal units. Generator Output already includes that factor. The shaft solver weights speed changes by force_emitter_max_force and has no torque or inertia in SI units, so it gives no charge-per-joule figure for mechanical work. The shipped realtime file sets electric_consumption_scale to 0.01, but the executable contains that name neither as ASCII nor as UTF-16LE text, and its effect was not recovered.

limitations: Electric storage and draw use internal charge units; Generator Output is internal charge per simulated second. Battery Charge reads a 0 to 1 fraction and electric port inspection shows the EMP-adjusted supply fraction, both without a unit. A conversion of internal charge to joules or watts was not recovered.

Shaft speed is RPS, and a simple shaft group mixes speeds weighted by force_emitter_max_force plus weight 1 for the group's previous speed. How arbitrary gearbox and clutch networks, conflicting ratio loops and connector rebuilds combine groups was not decoded, and the model gives no SI torque or inertia.
Static analysis only.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

categories.summary: Classic diesel engines share one recovered update. Above 2 RPS an undamaged engine with effective throttle u at local speed r submits 0.99 × (r + 0.1 × u × (r + 1)) RPS to its shaft. engine_max_force (20000, 60000, 200000) scales shaft weight and diesel use in the ratio 1 : 3 : 10. Heating before cooling is 0.0075 × |r| °C per update for every size.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Throttle is clamped to 0 to 1; a negative value counts as 0, so the engine never drives backward. Above the RPS Limiter (default 20 RPS, editor range 5 to 100) the throttle is cut to 0. That is a fuel cut, not a speed clamp: the engine can overshoot, and another component can spin the shaft faster. A damaged engine compares against 1.25 times the limit. Max Power (0 to 100 %) scales diesel use, intake and shaft weight together. Holding Starter draws electricity and pushes the engine toward 5 RPS. Fuel, air, cold and hot coolant and exhaust each have their own connection; the RPS and Temperature outputs report the engine's speed and temperature.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: engine_max_force F is 20000, 60000 and 200000 for the small, medium and large diesel. The update uses it as a shaft weight W = F × Max Power ÷ 2000 (10, 30 and 100), as the diesel and intake demand scale s = F × Max Power ÷ 20000 (1, 3 and 10), and in the starter's charge request. At the same RPS and throttle every size gains speed and heats at the same rate. The bigger engine counts 3 or 10 times as much in the shaft's weighted average, so it holds speed better under load, and burns 3 or 10 times the diesel. W and the speed steps are internal solver quantities, not N m, watts or joules.

sections.title: Speed, fuel and heat
sections.body:
With local speed r in RPS and effective throttle u, the speed factor is g(r) = 1 ÷ (0.03 × r + 0.05) + 0.4 × r - 6. Diesel use is 0.012 × s × u × r × g(r) L/s. At full throttle and 10 RPS that is 0.102857, 0.308571 and 1.028571 L/s for the small, medium and large engine; at 20 RPS 0.849231, 2.547692 and 8.492308 L/s, so fuel use climbs steeply with speed. u is the throttle after the limiter and EMP cuts, reduced further when diesel, oxygen or the intake-over-exhaust pressure margin runs short. Full throttle needs air with 21 % oxygen and an intake pressure at least 2 above the exhaust; at a margin of 1 or less the engine gets no air. With infinite_fuel on, the diesel, air and exhaust exchange is skipped.

Each update the engine submits r_submit = 0.99 × (r + 0.1 × u × (r + 1)) to its shaft. Combustion adds speed only above 2 RPS; below that only the 0.99 retention applies, although the fuel formula still runs. At 10 RPS and full throttle the submitted speed is 10.989 RPS. Combustion outpaces the 1 % loss at every speed once u is about 0.101 or more, so an engine with nothing else on its shaft speeds up until the limiter cuts the throttle. The limiter, not the throttle, sets its free-running speed.

Heating is 0.0075 × |r| °C per update, 0.45 × |r| per simulated second, before cooling: 4.5 °C/s at 10 RPS for every size. It does not depend on throttle directly, so a shaft driven by another engine heats this one at zero throttle.

sections.title: Shaft and load
sections.body: The engine writes W and r_submit to its shaft group and takes back the group speed. A simple group mixes (R + Σ W_i × r_i) ÷ (1 + Σ W_i), where R is the group's previous speed. Several engines on one shaft therefore pull it toward their submitted speeds in proportion to W. The RPS output shows the local speed entering the update, before this update's starter and combustion steps.

sections.title: Cooling and overheating
sections.body:
Each engine holds 100 L of fresh water coolant at start. Each update the coolant ports exchange fluid, then engine and coolant move toward each other: with liquid coolant they meet halfway (factor 0.5), with gas or empty coolant not at all. The engine then moves 0.001 of the way toward the surrounding temperature. The hot output gets a pump bias of 0.1 × |r|, at most 2; the cold return has none. Example: everything at 20 °C, 10 RPS, liquid coolant: the engine ends the update at 20.0374625 °C instead of 20.074925 °C without coolant.

Above 115 °C, with engine_overheating on and a second settings flag set, the engine takes 1 damage at once and 1 more every 300 updates (5 simulated seconds), up to 50. Damage 1 to 19 cuts the combustion gain from 0.1 to 0.06; from 20 combustion adds no speed while fuel and heat continue.

sections.title: Starter
sections.body: While Starter is held the engine requests max(5 - r, 0) × W × electric_magnitude × 0.1 charge: 1.2, 3.6 and 12 per RPS below 5 for the small, medium and large engine, 6, 18 and 60 from rest. It adds the supplied fraction of the deficit to its speed, so full supply lifts it to 5 RPS in one update before shaft mixing. A loaded shaft pulls it back, and above 5 RPS the starter asks for nothing.

sections.title: Legacy turbine
sections.body: The Turbine Engine part (turbine.xml) runs this same update with engine_max_force 100000, shaft weight 50. It ships with no fuel, air, coolant or exhaust port and electric_magnitude 0, so its supply gate and starter stay at 0; see its own article.

limitations: The classic update 0x14034ba00 was decoded by static analysis of one build; the game was not run. A conversion of the shaft weight and speed steps to SI torque in N m, watts or joules was not recovered.

Engine temperature depends on RPS history, coolant flow and the surrounding-temperature sample; the sampler's weather and environment inputs were not decoded, so no single temperature per throttle setting exists.
The settings byte that forms the second overheat gate (settings+0x4a) was not traced to a named option.
Behaviour with the shaft spinning backward or at non-finite speeds was not established. Thermal efficiency in physical units is unknown.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

categories.summary: Each connected run of open or enclosed pipe is one 40 L network; pumps add a pressure bias, which caps equal-pressure flow at 200 L/s for the small electric pump, 400 L/s for the large one and 60 L/s for the manual pump; tanks, hoses, connectors and filters move fluid between networks without merging them; fluid meters use one channel per fluid type.

sections.title: Moving fluid
sections.body:
Every connected run of ordinary or enclosed pipe is one network compartment of volume 4, 40 L, however many pipe blocks it spans. Both pipe kinds have type 6 and join the same network. For clean water its pressure is 15 × the stored amount, 60 when full. Each update the network shares its fluid and free room among the demands its ports set on the previous update, and each port then moves at most half its demand.

A pump adds its bias to the pressure difference. Electric pumps use electrical supply × pump_pressure × Max Power, impeller pumps 4 × |RPS| × pump_pressure, and the modular engine fluid pump its own shaft speed. At equal pressure the move is at most min(bias, 20) ÷ 30 amount per update: 200 L/s for the small electric pump (pump_pressure 10), 400 L/s for the large one (100), and no pump exceeds 400 L/s. The flow readout shows 1 amount per update as 600 L/s, 10 L per amount. The manual pump (pump_pressure 3) pushes one-way with bias 3 while an interact action is held, with a smoothed handle factor h from 0 to 1 as its step factor; at h = 1 its bound is 60 L/s.

Tanks, hoses, connectors and filters keep their networks separate and move fluid between them each update. A tank exchanges each port's network with its own compartment at factor 1. The old coiled Hose, the mechanical winches, rope-hook hoses, hose pulleys, fluid connectors and filters link two networks through the two-port solver with bias 0 in both directions. Their factor, 1 for the Hose, mechanical winches, hose pulleys and filters and 0.5 for rope-hook hoses and fluid connectors, scales the per-update step limit. None of these links reads hose length or adds hose volume; a hose pulley shares one 40 L network between its two ports.

sections.title: Pressure
sections.body:
All 13 fluid types use one pressure law; only gas or liquid matters. Gases are the air slot, CO2, steam, oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen; the rest are liquids. With L and G the liquid and gas amounts in a compartment of volume V: up to V = 8 (80 L), P = 60 × (L + G) ÷ V. Above 8, P = 7.5 × (G × min(1, 8 ÷ (V − L)) + max(L × 4 ÷ (60 × V), L − V + 8)).

Pure gas gives 60 × amount ÷ V at any volume. Pure liquid in a compartment above volume 8 reads under 0.5 atm until less than 80 L of room is left, then rises 7.5 atm per 75 L to 60 when full. Pressure outputs are in atmospheres. pump_pressure adds to the same scale inside the solver, but no unit or delivered head is documented for it.

sections.title: Temperature carried with fluid
sections.body: Fluid arriving in a compartment is mixed by the compartment's amount after the move: T = (A' × T + q × T_donor) ÷ (A' + q). So 1 unit at 20 °C receiving 0.5 at 100 °C ends at 40 °C, not the 46.7 °C of ordinary mixing. Below 0.01 amount per update, radiator, manifold and two-way pump ports also exchange temperature directly at a rate of up to 0.1 ÷ volume per update, so heat crosses a port even with no net flow.

sections.title: Storage and temperature
sections.body:
Each listed voxel of a tank gives 15.625 L. Liquid tanks hold 31.25, 187.5 and 703.125 L and gas tanks 46.875, 109.375, 984.375 and 3515.625 L. Tanks keep their contents' temperature and drift toward the surrounding temperature by 0.001 per update. At 60 updates per simulated second that leaves 0.942 of the gap after one second, a time constant of 16.7 s.

A fresh gas tank starts at 59.4 atm at full fill. The fluid spawner fills its enclosing custom compartment with up to 0.99 × fill × volume, limited by free room; its tooltip says gases are spawned at 60 atm. A custom compartment's volume follows its geometry rather than the pipe network's 4.

sections.title: Identifying fluids
sections.body: The liquid and gas meters share one composite layout: 1 water, 2 diesel, 3 jet fuel, 4 air, 5 CO2, 6 oil, 7 seawater, 8 steam, 9 slurry, 10 saturated slurry, 11 oxygen, 12 nitrogen, 13 hydrogen. Air is reported as the sum of oxygen, carbon dioxide and nitrogen.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: The shipped realtime file lists gas and liquid base damping 0.99 and 0.9999, but none of the four fluid damping names occurs in the executable, so no setting binding was recovered. To test for an effect, compare two values of a setting on the same layout and starting inventory. Check Flow Rate against the solver bounds on the actual network graph: pipe length adds no volume, and hoses and connectors link networks at factor 1 or 0.5. Check a prefab gas tank's start (59.4 atm decoded) separately from a fluid-spawner compartment (60 atm in its tooltip).

limitations: Native coverage for this build: ordinary and enclosed pipe networks, fixed liquid and gas tanks, the electric, impeller, modular and manual pumps, both filters, the old Hose and mechanical winches, rope-hook hoses, hose pulleys and the fluid connector. Custom-compartment volume from wall geometry and hull flooding were not decoded. Diesel and jet-fuel tank startup, startup from saved inventory, handheld hose free ends, slurry processing and steam or seawater behaviour outside the selected phase-change callers were not traced. The four realtime fluid damping names do not occur in the executable, so their effect on this build was not recovered.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

categories.summary: Exchangers mix two compartments of 0.5 × listed voxels each, moving 0.03 of the gap per update weighted by each side's stored gas or liquid amount; radiators cool toward the surroundings and gain up to three times their passive rate from an electric fan or airflow.

sections.title: How the game moves heat
sections.body:
Every exchanger has two mixed compartments, A and B, each of volume V = 0.5 × the definition's listed voxels, 10 L per volume unit. Per side that is 20, 250 and 1215 L for the air-air sizes, 10, 50, 225, 405 and 1125 L for air-liquid, and 20 and 125 L for liquid-liquid. Each update, when qA + qB > 0.001, A moves toward B by 0.03 × qB ÷ (qA + qB) of the old gap and B toward A by 0.03 × qA ÷ (qA + qB). q is the stored amount of the side's phase: gas slots 3, 4, 7, 10, 11 and 12 on an air side, liquid slots 0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 8 and 9 on a liquid side, each species with weight 1. At equal fill and gas pressure a larger variant has proportionally more q; the 0.03 fraction is the same for all of them.

Both compartments then move 0.001 toward the filtered surrounding temperature. Radiators use a separate rule: the compartment moves toward the surrounding temperature by 0.003 × (1 + fan), with the fan term clamped to 0…2.

sections.title: Capacity and pressure
sections.body: q is in native amount units: 1 amount is 10 L of liquid, or 600 L of gas at the expanded readout. For pure gas q = P × V ÷ 60, so doubling an air side's pressure doubles its q. At 1 atm a gas side has q = V ÷ 60, against V for a full liquid side of the same volume; at 60 atm the two match. The capacity helpers apply no pressure, temperature or per-species factor of their own. Fluid of the wrong phase counts 0 toward that side's q but still passes through the ports and raises pressure.

sections.title: Ports and through-flow
sections.body: Each update runs four port exchanges before the heat step, in the order A In, A Out, B In, B Out, all with bias 0 and no species filter. A side moves fluid only when both of its ports are connected; the heat step runs either way. B Out uses an exchange factor of clamp(0.5 × B's total amount, 0, 1). The exchanger has no pump and its In and Out labels do not set a direction, so pressure and the networks' demand decide which way fluid goes. Arriving fluid is mixed by the compartment's amount after the move, and below 0.01 amount per update a direct port exchange also carries heat without net flow. Each side is a single mixed volume, so there is no counterflow or parallel-flow geometry.

sections.title: Per-second rates
sections.body: Component updates run 60 times per simulated second. The fractions compound, so they are not multiplied by 60. With constant coefficients and nothing else acting, one simulated second leaves 0.161 of the gap between an exchanger's two compartments (time constant 0.547 s), 0.942 of a gap to fixed ambient through the leak alone (16.7 s), 0.835 of a passive radiator's gap to fixed ambient (5.55 s) and 0.581 at the full radiator multiplier of 3 (1.84 s). Through-flow and changing temperatures need the full model stepped 60 times per second.

sections.title: Surrounding temperature
sections.body: An exchanger samples the surrounding temperature at its own position every 16 updates (0.267 simulated seconds). Outside a compartment the sample blends the air and water weather temperatures by w = clamp((h − y + 0.25) ÷ 24, 0, 1), with h the wave-surface height and y the sample height, so it is pure air from 0.25 above the surface and pure water from 23.75 below it. Inside an enclosed compartment the compartment's temperature replaces the weather. Nearby heat sources then raise the sample, toward at most 400. A linear controller ramps to each new sample over 16 updates.

sections.title: Practical setup
sections.body: Connect both ports of a side. The exchanger pushes fluid through a side only when its In and Out ports are both connected, and a radiator cools only when both of its fluid ports are connected. A radiator outside any enclosed compartment counts relative airflow as fan, reaching the maximum term at an air speed of 80 in the game's speed units (2 × 40). Inside a compartment that bonus is skipped and the reference temperature is the compartment's.

limitations: Native findings come from static decompilation of one build; no in-game measurement was made.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

The exchanged quantity is a native amount × temperature unit; no conversion to joules or watts was recovered. No installation-independent effectiveness curve exists in the code: outlet temperatures depend on actual flow, fill, gas pressure, ambient and the connected networks.
The complete set of local heat sources that feed the surrounding-temperature sample, and their strengths, was not traced.

categories.summary: Storage units recharge stored equipment from vehicle power; tooltips give concrete limits such as 230 m diving depth for 10 minutes, scuba 40 m for 2 minutes and 500 m handheld radio range.

sections.title: Equipment limits
sections.body: Diving gear reaches 230 m with 10 minutes of air; scuba reaches 40 m with 2 minutes. Handheld radios and remotes use frequencies 0~8 with 500 m effective range. Firefighting and hazmat gear absorb 95% of fire or radiation damage.

limitations: Tooltip statements only.

categories.summary: Modular jets run on internal pressure: the powered compressor builds it, the chamber above 0.5 RPS adds 1600 × throttle × RPS and burns 0.12 × throttle × RPS L/s of jet fuel, turbines turn half of it into RPS, and exhausts push with 32 × (pressure - 1000).

sections.title: How a jet runs
sections.body:
Every jet part keeps an incoming and an outgoing pressure and temperature. Each update a compressor, chamber, turbine or exhaust first averages them with its neighbours, then: the compressor moves q = 0.2 × (100 × r0 - (p_out - p_in)) from its incoming to its outgoing side; the chamber, above 0.5 RPS, sets p_out = p_in + 1600 × u × r and t_out = t_in + 0.1 × u × r; a turbine passes on half of its incoming pressure and gains 0.0000375 × p_in RPS; an exhaust above 1000 pushes with 32 × (p_in - 1000). r is RPS and u the effective throttle.

After all updates the intakes, compressors, chambers and turbines joined through those neighbour lists average their RPS, so the compressor's spin and the turbines' gain feed the chamber's RPS. Exhausts take no part in this.

sections.title: Starting
sections.body: Turn on the compressor's Compressor input and connect electricity. Each update it requests 0.1 charge, 6 per simulated second, and with full supply gains 0.01 RPS before its 0.99 retention and pressure load. The chamber ignites once its RPS is above 0.5; the tooltip's internal pressure threshold does not exist in the decoded branch. Throttle 0 to 1 sets u.

sections.title: Thrust
sections.body: Exhaust force = 32 × (incoming pressure - 1000) × altitude factor × afterburner multiplier × (1 - Thrust Spoiler), before a cap of 100 × S, with S a per-vehicle scale. RPS enters only through the pressure the chamber adds, so the tooltip's proportionality to internal RPS describes the chain, not the exhaust formula. The altitude factor 1 - height × 1.5 ÷ 40000 reaches 0 at a height of 26666.67, metres if the height field is in metres, which is an inference. The three exhausts use the same coefficient; the rotating one only changes direction.

sections.title: Fuel
sections.body: The chamber burns 0.12 × u × RPS L/s, 2.4 L/s at 20 RPS and full throttle, from a 4 L buffer fed by its Fuel port; a short buffer lowers u. An enabled afterburner multiplies thrust by 1 + 500 × the jet fuel amount in its own buffer, 1.5 at 0.01 L. Its branch never subtracts that fuel.

sections.title: Units
sections.body: Pressure, temperature, charge and force are the game's internal units. The force is applied once per update and integrated by the physics solver; do not multiply it by 60. The medium turbine's shaft weight of 160 is a solver weight, not a torque in N m.

limitations: Static decompilation of one build; the game was not run. How ducts, splitters and merged assemblies build the neighbour lists was not traced, so the equilibrium pressure, RPS and thrust of an assembled engine and its startup time are not predicted from a parts list.

Physical units of jet pressure and temperature were not established; pressure, temperature, charge and force stay in internal units. How the game builds the cap scale S for craft joined by locked joints was not decoded, so forces near the cap are not predicted.
SI torque, power and efficiency were not recovered. Intake behaviour was not decoded.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

categories.summary: All logic gates run in one native update, once per update. Boolean gates are plain; latches and flip-flops act only when an input changes; timers count whole updates; numeric outputs replace NaN and infinity with 0.

sections.title: How logic updates
sections.body: Each gate is one case of the logic update, chosen by its logic_gate_type through a jump table. The component dispatcher calls it once per component per update, 60 times per simulated second. A case computes its outputs from the input values it holds at that moment and adds no delay of its own.

sections.title: Numeric outputs
sections.body: Arithmetic is single precision. Numeric gates pass their result through a finite-value check that turns NaN and ±infinity into 0. That check does not limit values to −1 … 1.

sections.title: Edge cases worth knowing
sections.body: Divide outputs 0 and turns Error on when |B| ≤ 1e-6; Modulo outputs 0 for the same divisor. Threshold is on when lower ≤ x ≤ upper. Greater Than is off when A equals B. Trigonometry works in turns, and asin or acos of |x| > 1 gives 0. The SR latch favours Reset. The JK flip-flop and SR latch act only on an update where an input changed, so holding both JK inputs on toggles once, not every update. Clear on the memory register restores the configured value.

sections.title: Timers count updates
sections.body: Delay, Blinker and Capacitor multiply their seconds by 60 and truncate to whole updates; 0.51 s becomes 30 updates. Counters and Up/Down step every update. The PID has no time step at all.

sections.title: Inside a microprocessor
sections.body: A microprocessor gathers every component's inputs before it runs any component, so a signal moves one component per update inside it (inference). Its PID, Blinker and timers are separate routines; see the PID Controller and Microprocessor pages.

limitations: Propagation latency between separate physical logic blocks was not traced: the step that copies one block's output into the next block's input, and its order across blocks and vehicles, was not located.
Sign, rounding and domain edge cases of the library helpers behind Modulo, Exponent and Trigonometry were not decoded.
The function block's expression language (operator set, parser, rounding and constant expressions) was not decoded.
Power Add and Power Meter do nothing in the logic update; their transmission-network formulas were not decoded.
Train Junction Controller routing, junction selection and the priority of conflicting requests were not traced.

Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

categories.summary: Powered pivots, hinges, turrets and sliders expose Speed, Max Power and a Gear Ratio of 1:1 to 1:32; robotic joints are limited to 0.25 turns either way while velocity joints and turret rings turn continuously.

sections.title: Joint properties
sections.body: Multibody components whose definition flags include 0x100 get a Max Power slider shown as a percentage and a Gear Ratio selector with 1:1, 1:2, 1:4, 1:8, 1:16 and 1:32. Robotic and velocity types additionally show a Speed slider.

sections.title: Choosing a joint
sections.body: Robotic pivots and hinges seek a target inside ±0.25 turns and report Current Rotation in that range. Velocity pivots and turret rings rotate continuously at the commanded speed, report rotation in turns, and stop at an input of 0. Turret rings also extend a sealed volume through the ring.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: How the gear ratio trades speed for holding torque and what Max Power scales were not recovered numerically; measure with a torque meter on a torque-capable joint.

limitations: The numeric effect of Gear Ratio and Max Power was not decoded.
Static analysis only.

categories.summary: Recovered cylinder code gives a concrete tuning target: keep the air:fuel ratio near 13.6–14.0, keep the crank below 60 RPS, keep manifolds under 115 °C and give the exhaust room.

sections.title: Combustion window
sections.body: Each cylinder computes a fuel term (RPS × 4e-6 × voxels × fuel throttle) and an intake term (RPS × 2.8e-6 × voxels ÷ 60 × air throttle × pressure factor). At 60 updates per simulated second the fuel term is RPS × 0.00024 × voxels × fuel throttle per second. The displayed air:fuel ratio is intake × 600 ÷ fuel, so with equal throttles and no boost it reads 7. Combustion happens only when the ratio lies between 12 − 2t and 16 + 4t, where t is manifold temperature ÷ 100 clamped to 0…1. Within the window the mixture factor 1 − 2(s − 0.6)² peaks at an air:fuel ratio of 13.6 cold and 14.0 when the manifold is at or above 100 °C.

sections.title: Speed, heat and damage
sections.body: Fuel admission is cut above 60 RPS, so cylinders act as a hard rev limiter. Speed efficiency falls from 1 at standstill to 0.5 at 50 RPS. Burning fuel heats the manifold group (gain 6000 ÷ heat capacity); above 115 °C, with engine overheating enabled, the cylinder takes damage every 300 updates (5 simulated seconds), and torque gain drops from 80000 to 40000 once damaged.

sections.title: Assembly
sections.body: Crank inertia is the sum of engine_max_force over the assembly: a 1x1 crank block adds 0.7 while flywheels add 150, 600 and 2400. Inertia divides every torque impulse, so flywheels smooth speed and make starting slower. The starter only pushes while the crank is below 5 RPS.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Compartment pressure units and the units of manifold heat and coolant transfer were not recovered; measure RPS response and temperatures in game to calibrate these.

limitations: All engine formulas are reconstructed from static decompilation of build f9206d85…; they were not checked in a running game.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.
Throttle offsets 0x88 and 0x90 are attributed to the fuel and air manifolds from the oxygen/diesel caps applied to them; the manifold write path was only partially traced.

categories.summary: This catch-all holds sensors, radios, lights, fluid fittings, connectors, winches, doors and tools; the most useful hard numbers are ranges, which the definitions confirm: v2 radios 100 m to 20 km with legacy radios configured identically, and radar ranges from 5000 to 500000 m.

sections.title: Radio ranges
sections.body: rx_range equals the tooltip's ground-level range on every v2 radio (100, 1000, 4000, 20000) and on the directional antennas (8000000, 10000000). The legacy radios carry the same rx_range values as their v2 counterparts, so expect the same ranges.

sections.title: Radar and sonar ranges
sections.body: radar_range matches the stated range for the basic radars (5000, 20000, 50000), sonars (3000, 1000), advanced sonars (60000, 100000, 200000) and the fish finder (100). The advanced radars without a stated range carry 60000 (radar), 500000 (AWACS), 200000 (dish), 100000 (phalanx) and 20000 (missile).

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Detection probability against target size and FOV for the advanced radars; radio signal strength against distance.

limitations: Range fields are configuration; detection and signal models were not decoded.
Unrelated definitions carry serialized default ranges; only sensor and radio definitions are interpreted here.

categories.summary: Propellers and rotors carry a force_emitter_max_force field that ranks variants (marine 20000 to 200000, rotors 40000 to 200000); marine propellers work only underwater and rotors lose force underwater.

sections.title: Variant ranking
sections.body: force_emitter_max_force: marine propellers 20000, 100000 and 200000; pitchable propellers 20000, 80000 and 160000; helicopter rotors 40000 and 200000; heavy rotors 120000 and 200000; ducted fans 2000 and 10000. Helicopter and through-drive rotors also carry force_emitter_efficiency 1.25 where most other emitters carry 1.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Marine propellers and the azimuth thruster operate only underwater; helicopter rotors produce less force underwater. Solid rocket boosters burn once; a slower burn-rate setting lasts longer but gives less thrust.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Whether force_emitter_max_force is a thrust cap and how RPS maps to thrust were not recovered; measure thrust against RPS with a fixed test rig.

limitations: Force-emitter fields are configuration; their runtime use was not decoded.

categories.summary: Pilot seats expose four axes from −1 to 1, six hotkeys, look angles in turns and a composite with fixed channels (on/off 31 trigger, 32 occupied; values 1–4 axes, 9–10 look).

sections.title: Composite layout
sections.body: On/Off 1 and up carry hotkeys, 31 the trigger and 32 occupancy; values 1–4 carry the axes and 9–10 the look direction. The HOTAS seat adds axes 5–8 and up to 48 hotkeys.

limitations: Port descriptions only.

categories.summary: Steam power chains a coal firebox, boiler, piston or turbine and condenser; duct sizes carry capacity fields 42.1875, 195.3125 and 351.5625.

sections.title: Chain
sections.body: The firebox consumes one coal to ignite and heats coolant; the boiler turns that heat into steam and should be throttled to hold steam pressure; pistons need pressure alternated between their couplings by piston position; the condenser must stay cooled.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Heat output per coal, boiler evaporation rate and piston torque against pressure.

limitations: Steam simulation code was not decoded.

categories.summary: Weight blocks shift the centre of mass; keels resist roll and lateral slip while submerged, letting sails drive a boat across or into the wind.

sections.title: Keels and skis
sections.body: Keels are the counterpart to sails; skis slide lengthwise and grip laterally.

limitations: Tooltip statements; keel force code was not decoded.

categories.summary: Gearboxes switch between two ratios picked from a fixed list of eight, including a 1:-1 reverse, and need electricity to change ratio.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Gearboxes use torque_component_type 1. Gear Switch off applies the Ratio Off selection, on applies Ratio On. The gearbox only changes ratio while it has electrical availability; without power it keeps the last ratio. Each change draws electricity.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Both ratios are chosen from eight fixed options, not typed numbers: 1:-1, 1:1, 6:5, 3:2, 9:5, 2:1, 5:2 and 3:1. Internally they become the multipliers -1, 1, 0.8333333, 0.6666667, 0.5555556, 0.5, 0.4 and 0.33333334; the coupling stores the reciprocal. 1:-1 reverses direction without changing speed.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Which side (RPS A or RPS B) turns faster for an N:1 option, and how much torque the coupling transmits before slipping, need an in-game torque meter test.

limitations: Ratio orientation (which port is the faster side) was not established.
Static analysis only.

categories.summary: Autocannon drums hold 100, 200 or 500 rounds and machine-gun boxes 100 or 400; barrels add accuracy and recoil, muzzle brakes cut recoil.

sections.title: Ammunition
sections.body: Drums hold one caliber each; machine-gun boxes take only kinetic, armour-piercing and incendiary rounds and must be refilled by hand. Autocannons need electricity to feed from belts or drums.

sections.title: Barrel tuning
sections.body: Barrel extensions increase accuracy but also recoil (some heavy and rotary barrels add weight instead); a muzzle brake at the end reduces recoil. Fuse Timer sets a delay in seconds for high-explosive and fragmentation rounds.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Spread and recoil per barrel extension, projectile velocity and damage.

limitations: Ballistics were not decoded.

categories.summary: Wheel radius fields (0.35 to 1.05 for road wheels) set ground speed per RPS if they are rolling radii in metres; track wheels only form tracks with matching wheels in line.

sections.title: Choosing a size
sections.body: Road wheels carry wheel_radius 0.35, 0.58, 0.85 and 1.05. The distance sensor tooltip equates one metre with four blocks, so if this is a rolling radius in metres the no-slip speed is 2π × radius × RPS: about 2.2 m/s per RPS for the smallest and 6.6 m/s per RPS for the largest.

sections.title: Tracks
sections.body: Track wheels form a track only with wheels of the same size and orientation placed in line on the same body; at least one drive wheel must receive power.

sections.title: Measurement questions
sections.body: Confirm the radius unit with a linear speed sensor at known RPS; measure slip under load.

limitations: The metre interpretation of wheel_radius is unverified; speed figures are no-slip geometry, not measurements.

categories.summary: Windows are geometry pieces; their definitions describe shape and placement only, and no window-specific behaviour was recovered.

sections.title: Placement
sections.body: Flat windows sit flush with walls; angled and corner pieces close gaps between angled windows.

limitations: No window-specific behaviour was located.

families.summary: Mixes two gas compartments of 20, 250 or 1215 L each, moving 0.03 of the gap per update weighted by stored gas amount, which rises with pressure.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Case 0x11 uses the gas capacity helper for both sides: q is the stored amount of the air slot, CO2, steam, oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen, each with weight 1. Liquid in a side counts 0. Each side passes gas only with both its In and Out ports connected.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: The per-update rule is the same as for the other exchangers: 0.03 of the gap, weighted by the opposite side's share of q, plus a 0.001 drift toward ambient. Without through-flow, 0.161 of the gap remains after one simulated second.

sections.title: Gas pressure
sections.body: For pure gas q = P × V ÷ 60, so doubling a side's pressure doubles its q and the lower-pressure side moves further toward the other. The helper adds no pressure or temperature factor of its own. If a side also holds liquid, its q is the gas amount alone, not P × V ÷ 60.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: The 2x2, 2x5 and 3x9 hold 2, 25 and 121.5 volume units per side (20, 250 and 1215 L), ratios 1, 12.5 and 60.75. The files are named heat_exchanger_2_2, heat_exchanger_5_5 and heat_exchanger_9_9; the listed voxel count, not the name, sets the volume.

sections.title: Flow example
sections.body: The 2x2 at 30 atm with 600 L/s of expanded gas through each side, inlets 100 and 20 °C and ambient 20 °C, emits 71.55 and 43.86 °C. Temp A and Temp B settle at 71.08 and 44.25 °C. These are outputs of the report's 60 Hz model with fixed boundary networks and a prescribed flow, not game measurements or a pump rating. The interactive graph below runs the same model.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Temp A and Temp B read the stored compartment temperatures in °C after this update's exchange and ambient step. Fluid leaving the Out ports was emitted earlier in the same update, so its temperature can differ. Both compartments also drift toward the surrounding temperature by 0.001 per update, so an idle exchanger slowly settles to ambient: the leak alone has a time constant of 16.7 simulated seconds.

findings.label: Exchanger step fraction
findings.detail: In water_component_type cases 0x10 (liquid-liquid), 0x11 (air-air) and 0x12 (air-liquid), compartment A moves toward B by fraction·qB/(qA+qB) and B toward A by fraction·qA/(qA+qB), where q is the per-side capacity value returned by the gas helper 0x1402eb660 or the liquid helper 0x1402eb5e0. findings.label: Exchanger capacity q
findings.value: pure gas q = P × V ÷ 60; liquid q = stored liquid amount
findings.detail: q is the side's stored amount of its phase in native units, 10 L of liquid or 600 L of expanded gas per amount. Inference from the pressure law: pure gas has P = 60 × G ÷ V, so q = G = P × V ÷ 60 and doubling pressure doubles q at a fixed volume. At equal volume a 1 atm gas side has V ÷ 60 and a full liquid side V; at 60 atm the gas side equals the full liquid side. With gas and liquid in one side, sum the gas amounts instead of using P × V ÷ 60. Wrong-phase contents give 0 toward that side's q but still move through the ports. Report: investigation/heat-exchangers.md. limitations: The exchanged quantity is a native amount × temperature unit; no conversion to joules or watts was recovered. No installation-independent effectiveness curve exists in the code: outlet temperatures depend on actual flow, fill, gas pressure, ambient and the connected networks.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Mixes a gas compartment and a liquid compartment of 10 to 1125 L each, moving 0.03 of the gap per update weighted by stored gas and liquid amount.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Case 0x12 of the fluid-component update treats side A as gas (Air In/Air Out) and side B as liquid (Fluid In/Fluid Out): qA is the stored gas amount and qB the stored liquid amount. A side passes fluid only when its In and Out ports are both connected; the A/B exchange runs whenever qA + qB > 0.001, with or without flow. Neither side has a species filter or a pump bias, so fluid can run either way through a port pair.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: Per update, A moves toward B by 0.03 × qB ÷ (qA + qB) and B toward A by 0.03 × qA ÷ (qA + qB). The air side holds q = P × V ÷ 60 and the liquid side its stored liquid, so below 60 atm the liquid usually has the larger q and the air moves further toward it. With no through-flow and no ambient leak, 0.161 of the gap remains after one simulated second (60 updates).

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: All five variants share the 0.03 fraction. Each side holds 10, 50, 225, 405 or 1125 L (V = 1, 5, 22.5, 40.5 and 112.5), so at equal liquid fill and gas pressure both q values scale by 1, 5, 22.5, 40.5 and 112.5 relative to the 1x2. The fraction of the gap closed per update does not change. At equal external flow a larger variant also holds more fluid and loses more to ambient, so the volume ratio is not an outlet-temperature ratio.

sections.title: Flow example
sections.body: The 1x2 with 100 °C air at 30 atm and 600 L/s of expanded gas on side A, and 20 °C liquid at 0.8 fill and 6 L/s on side B, ambient 20 °C, emits air at 79.80 °C and liquid at 47.71 °C. Temp A and Temp B settle at 79.15 and 48.06 °C. These are outputs of the report's 60 Hz model with fixed boundary networks and a prescribed flow, not game measurements or a pump rating. The interactive graph below runs the same model.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Temp A and Temp B read the stored compartment temperatures in °C after this update's exchange and ambient step. Fluid leaving the Out ports was emitted earlier in the same update, so its temperature can differ. Both compartments also drift toward the surrounding temperature by 0.001 per update, so an idle exchanger slowly settles to ambient: the leak alone has a time constant of 16.7 simulated seconds.

findings.label: Exchanger capacity q
findings.value: pure gas q = P × V ÷ 60; liquid q = stored liquid amount
findings.detail: q is the side's stored amount of its phase in native units, 10 L of liquid or 600 L of expanded gas per amount. Inference from the pressure law: pure gas has P = 60 × G ÷ V, so q = G = P × V ÷ 60 and doubling pressure doubles q at a fixed volume. At equal volume a 1 atm gas side has V ÷ 60 and a full liquid side V; at 60 atm the gas side equals the full liquid side. With gas and liquid in one side, sum the gas amounts instead of using P × V ÷ 60. Wrong-phase contents give 0 toward that side's q but still move through the ports. Report: investigation/heat-exchangers.md. limitations: The exchanged quantity is a native amount × temperature unit; no conversion to joules or watts was recovered. No installation-independent effectiveness curve exists in the code: outlet temperatures depend on actual flow, fill, gas pressure, ambient and the connected networks.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Force scales linearly with rudder_surface_area, so medium and large fins make 4 and 6 times the force of the small one under the same conditions. Fins have smaller area and deflection than control surfaces, suiting fine trim.

sections.title: Air force
sections.body: Fins use the same routine as control surfaces, with rudder_type 0 and no wing term: force = 24 × area × P × B × (1 - immersion) × (airspeed - 15) × normal airspeed, above 15 m/s.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Force scales linearly with rudder_surface_area, so medium and large surfaces make 2.8 and 7 times the force of the small one under the same conditions. All sizes share the 45° limit and the -1 to 1 Rotation input.

sections.title: Air force
sections.body: Control surfaces have rudder_type 0, so there is no wing term: force = 24 × area × P × B × (1 - immersion) × (airspeed - 15) × normal airspeed, above 15 m/s. A surface edge-on to the airflow makes no force.

sections.title: Deflection speed
sections.body: Moving the surface draws electricity in proportion to the requested change. With full supply it reaches the requested angle in one update; with partial supply it moves part of the way.

families.summary: Small, medium and large diesel engines share one update: shaft weight 10, 30 and 100 and diesel use in the ratio 1 : 3 : 10 at the same RPS and throttle, with 0.102857, 0.308571 and 1.028571 L/s at 10 RPS and full throttle.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Throttle is clamped to 0 to 1; a negative value counts as 0, so the engine never drives backward. Above the RPS Limiter (default 20 RPS, editor range 5 to 100) the throttle is cut to 0. That is a fuel cut, not a speed clamp: the engine can overshoot, and another component can spin the shaft faster. A damaged engine compares against 1.25 times the limit. Max Power (0 to 100 %) scales diesel use, intake and shaft weight together. Holding Starter draws electricity and pushes the engine toward 5 RPS. Fuel, air, cold and hot coolant and exhaust each have their own connection; the RPS and Temperature outputs report the engine's speed and temperature.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: engine_max_force F is 20000, 60000 and 200000 for the small, medium and large diesel. The update uses it as a shaft weight W = F × Max Power ÷ 2000 (10, 30 and 100), as the diesel and intake demand scale s = F × Max Power ÷ 20000 (1, 3 and 10), and in the starter's charge request. At the same RPS and throttle every size gains speed and heats at the same rate. The bigger engine counts 3 or 10 times as much in the shaft's weighted average, so it holds speed better under load, and burns 3 or 10 times the diesel. W and the speed steps are internal solver quantities, not N m, watts or joules.

sections.title: Speed, fuel and heat
sections.body:
With local speed r in RPS and effective throttle u, the speed factor is g(r) = 1 ÷ (0.03 × r + 0.05) + 0.4 × r - 6. Diesel use is 0.012 × s × u × r × g(r) L/s. At full throttle and 10 RPS that is 0.102857, 0.308571 and 1.028571 L/s for the small, medium and large engine; at 20 RPS 0.849231, 2.547692 and 8.492308 L/s, so fuel use climbs steeply with speed. u is the throttle after the limiter and EMP cuts, reduced further when diesel, oxygen or the intake-over-exhaust pressure margin runs short. Full throttle needs air with 21 % oxygen and an intake pressure at least 2 above the exhaust; at a margin of 1 or less the engine gets no air. With infinite_fuel on, the diesel, air and exhaust exchange is skipped.

Each update the engine submits r_submit = 0.99 × (r + 0.1 × u × (r + 1)) to its shaft. Combustion adds speed only above 2 RPS; below that only the 0.99 retention applies, although the fuel formula still runs. At 10 RPS and full throttle the submitted speed is 10.989 RPS. Combustion outpaces the 1 % loss at every speed once u is about 0.101 or more, so an engine with nothing else on its shaft speeds up until the limiter cuts the throttle. The limiter, not the throttle, sets its free-running speed.

Heating is 0.0075 × |r| °C per update, 0.45 × |r| per simulated second, before cooling: 4.5 °C/s at 10 RPS for every size. It does not depend on throttle directly, so a shaft driven by another engine heats this one at zero throttle.

sections.title: Shaft and load
sections.body: The engine writes W and r_submit to its shaft group and takes back the group speed. A simple group mixes (R + Σ W_i × r_i) ÷ (1 + Σ W_i), where R is the group's previous speed. Several engines on one shaft therefore pull it toward their submitted speeds in proportion to W. The RPS output shows the local speed entering the update, before this update's starter and combustion steps.

sections.title: Cooling and overheating
sections.body:
Each engine holds 100 L of fresh water coolant at start. Each update the coolant ports exchange fluid, then engine and coolant move toward each other: with liquid coolant they meet halfway (factor 0.5), with gas or empty coolant not at all. The engine then moves 0.001 of the way toward the surrounding temperature. The hot output gets a pump bias of 0.1 × |r|, at most 2; the cold return has none. Example: everything at 20 °C, 10 RPS, liquid coolant: the engine ends the update at 20.0374625 °C instead of 20.074925 °C without coolant.

Above 115 °C, with engine_overheating on and a second settings flag set, the engine takes 1 damage at once and 1 more every 300 updates (5 simulated seconds), up to 50. Damage 1 to 19 cuts the combustion gain from 0.1 to 0.06; from 20 combustion adds no speed while fuel and heat continue.

sections.title: Starter
sections.body: While Starter is held the engine requests max(5 - r, 0) × W × electric_magnitude × 0.1 charge: 1.2, 3.6 and 12 per RPS below 5 for the small, medium and large engine, 6, 18 and 60 from rest. It adds the supplied fraction of the deficit to its speed, so full supply lifts it to 5 RPS in one update before shaft mixing. A loaded shaft pulls it back, and above 5 RPS the starter asks for nothing.

findings.label: Component updates per simulated second
findings.detail: One component update per component, then one physics tick that advances simulated time by 1/60 s. This holds for active, normally simulated vehicles; pauses, sleep or fast-forward, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside it. Report: investigation/update-rate.md. findings.detail: s = engine_max_force ÷ 20000 and W = engine_max_force ÷ 2000 = 10 × s at Max Power 100 %: small 1 and 10; medium 3 and 30; large 10 and 100. Fuel demand and shaft weight scale 1 : 3 : 10; Max Power scales both together. Report: investigation/classic-engines.md. findings.label: Speed step at 10 RPS, full throttle
findings.value: submitted 10.989 RPS; local step 0.989 RPS per update; weighted step 9.89 (small)
findings.detail: Undamaged, u = 1, r = 10: r_submit = 0.99 × (10 + 0.1 × 11) = 10.989. limitations: The classic update 0x14034ba00 was decoded by static analysis of one build; the game was not run. A conversion of the shaft weight and speed steps to SI torque in N m, watts or joules was not recovered.

Engine temperature depends on RPS history, coolant flow and the surrounding-temperature sample; the sampler's weather and environment inputs were not decoded, so no single temperature per throttle setting exists.
The settings byte that forms the second overheat gate (settings+0x4a) was not traced to a named option.
Behaviour with the shaft spinning backward or at non-finite speeds was not established. Thermal efficiency in physical units is unknown.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Capacity is electric_charge_capacity (1600, 12800, 256000). Each update a battery lends at most 10 × its charge fraction to the network pool, so more batteries supply more per update while a bigger battery lasts longer.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: The medium battery stores 8 times and the large 160 times the small battery's charge. All three lend the same packet of at most 10 per update, 600 per simulated second when full.

sections.title: Charge and discharge
sections.body:
A lone battery with nothing else on the network can give at most 10 × b per update, where b is its fraction, so a load that takes everything leaves b × (1 − 10 ÷ C) after each update. After one simulated second of that the small, medium and large battery keep 0.686, 0.954 and 0.998 of their charge. With N equally charged batteries, no generation and no other load, a request R gets q × min(1, 10 × N ÷ R) of what it asks.

Charging has no cap of its own. A deposit Q into a lone battery's pool raises its fraction by Q ÷ C up to full, and the surplus is lost. An idle lone battery loses nothing, because the loan and the return cancel. Batteries sharing a network move toward the pool fraction q by 10 × (q − b) ÷ C per update, so a small battery evens out faster than a large one.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Set Charge Level (0 to 100) in the properties to spawn partially charged. Charge outputs the stored fraction from 0 to 1. The game computes it as clamp(b ÷ ((C − 10) ÷ C), 0, 1) from the fraction left after the pool loan, which for a lone battery is the fraction before the update. While a battery is damaged the update sets its stored fraction, capacity and Charge to 0, so its charge is lost.

findings.label: Battery fraction change per update
findings.detail: For batteries (C above 10) the loan removes 10 × b ÷ C of the fraction and the return adds 10 × q ÷ C, with q = E ÷ P after draws and deposits. A lone idle battery has q = b and does not change. A load that empties the pool leaves b × (1 - 10 ÷ C). A deposit Q into a lone battery's pool raises b by Q ÷ C up to the clamp at 1. Batteries sharing a pool move toward q, a small battery faster than a large one. For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Pushes fluid with a bias of electrical supply × pump_pressure × Max Power; at equal pressure the small pump moves at most 200 L/s and the large one 400 L/s.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: The pump needs power and the On/Off signal. Each update it calls the two-port solver with bias = electrical supply × pump_pressure × Max Power. Supply is the share of its electricity request it receives, 1 with unlimited electricity, and Max Power defaults to 100 %. The pump is one-way: it never pushes fluid backward. It holds no fluid itself; its ports connect straight to the pipe networks. Off or damaged, it passes nothing. It requests 0.001 × Max Power electricity per update, the same for both sizes.

sections.title: Flow
sections.body:
At equal pressure on both sides the move is at most min(bias, 20) ÷ 30 amount per update. That is 200 L/s for the small pump and 400 L/s for the large one at full power. The large pump's bias reaches 20 at 20 % Max Power, so it keeps the 400 L/s bound down to that setting. The small pump reaches 200 L/s only at full power, though pressure from upstream can push more through it.

These are bounds. Real flow falls with fill, backpressure and other ports on the same network. In the report's reference loop with one 3x3 radiator, the small pump settled at 42.6 L/s and the large one at 165.5 L/s. The cooling capacity calculator's finite-flow mode steps such loops.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: pump_pressure 100 against 10 gives the large pump a tenfold bias, but the solver caps any bias above 20, so at full power its bound is twice the small pump's, not ten times.

sections.title: Open measurement questions
sections.body: Compare Flow Rate in game with the bounds above and with the finite-flow estimate for the same loop.

families.summary: Cools its fluid toward the surrounding temperature at 0.003 × (1 + fan) per update; the electric fan can triple the passive rate.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: Cooling runs only while both Fluid A and Fluid B are connected. The fan term is 2 × the electrical availability while Fan On/Off is on and power is present; each powered update also draws 0.001 units through the shared electricity helper, 0.06 units per simulated second.

sections.title: Performance drivers
sections.body: Cooling multiplier = 1 + fan, with fan clamped to 0…2, so a fully powered fan gives three times the passive rate. Mounted outside an enclosed compartment, relative airflow counts as fan as speed ÷ 40, so a fast vehicle reaches full cooling without power. The term alone leaves 0.835 of the gap to ambient after one simulated second at multiplier 1 and 0.581 at multiplier 3.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: Both sizes run the same rule and fraction. The compartment volume equals the listed voxels: 9 for the 3x3 and 25 for the 5x5, at 10 L per unit. The larger radiator therefore cools more stored water per update, if the pump keeps it filled.

sections.title: Flow through the radiator
sections.body:
Each update the radiator exchanges with its Fluid A network, then its Fluid B network, then cools. Arriving water is mixed by the radiator's amount after the move, and below 0.01 amount per update a direct exchange also moves temperature through the ports. Its volume is capacity: in a pumped loop it need not stay full, and its water settles cooler than the coolant manifold.

For one radiator fed at a fixed inlet temperature with flow q and stored water A, the outlet sits q ÷ (k × A + (1 + k) × q) of the way from ambient to the inlet, with k = 0.003 × (1 + fan). With 9 units of water, 200 L/s and a full fan that is 83.90 °C out for 100 °C in at 20 °C ambient, a 16.10 °C drop. The cooling capacity calculator's finite-flow mode steps whole loops.

sections.title: Open measurement questions

findings.label: Radiator outlet at fixed flow
findings.value: T_out - T_amb = q ÷ (k × A + (1 + k) × q) × (T_in - T_amb)
findings.detail: One radiator receiving q per update from an inlet at fixed temperature, discharging q, then cooling with k = 0.003 × (1 + fan), with water amount A after discharge and q ≥ 0.01: mixing weight q ÷ (A + 2q) = 0.034483 for the example below. Stored radiator temperature after the cooling step = (1 - k) × the same fraction. limitations: The airflow quantity is read as relative air speed from the vector-length call it is derived from; its unit was not confirmed.

For active, normally simulated vehicles, these formulas run once per nominal 1/60-second simulation update. Multiply per-update amounts by 60 for amounts per simulated second. A constant relaxation fraction k leaves (1-k)^60 of a gap after one simulated second. Physics solver substeps and render frames are separate; pauses, sleeping, unloaded vehicles and real-time slowdown are outside this conversion.

families.summary: Each update the motor takes a speed step of at most 2 × |Throttle| RPS and requests |step| × electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1 in charge: 0.24, 6.6 and 26.25 per RPS of step for the small, medium and large motor.

sections.title: How the update works
sections.body: With s = Throttle clamped to −1…1, the step is Δ = (20 × sign(s) − speed) × |s|, clamped to −2|s| … 2|s|. Δ is dropped when its sign differs from the throttle's, so a motor running faster than 20 RPS in the throttle direction is not held back, while reversing the throttle drives it toward −20. At zero throttle it only coasts. The motor requests |Δ| × electric_magnitude × force_emitter_max_force × 0.1, multiplies Δ by the fraction supplied, adds it, and then keeps 0.995 of its speed. With a shaft link it submits that speed and force_emitter_max_force to its shaft group and takes the group's published speed back. A damaged motor targets 0; the same step sign gate still applies.

sections.title: Variant tradeoffs
sections.body: At the full-throttle step of 2, the small, medium and large motor request 0.48, 13.2 and 52.5 per update. While the step stays at that bound, that is 28.8, 792 and 3150 per simulated second; supply limits the actual draw. Per unit of force_emitter_max_force the cost is 0.12, 0.11 and 0.105. The shaft group weights each part's speed by that force, so the small motor pays 1.1429 times and the medium 1.0476 times what the large one pays for the same force-weighted speed change.

sections.title: Battery supply
sections.body: Each full battery lends at most 10 per update to the pool. Without generation or other loads, the full-step requests need 1, 2 and 6 full batteries for the small, medium and large motor; a large motor on one full battery gets at most 0.1905 of its full-step request. A small step near the 20 RPS target asks for much less.

sections.title: What the cost tracks
sections.body: Charge scales with the speed step, not with speed × step. A given RPS change costs the same at low and high shaft speed, so equal charge buys equal force-weighted speed change rather than equal mechanical work. The shaft solver is a weighted average with no torque or inertia in SI units, so it gives no charge-per-joule figure.

sections.title: Setup and interactions
sections.body: Throttle limits the step, not the target speed: the target is always 20 RPS. Without a shaft link the update settles at 19.9 RPS at full throttle. At zero throttle an unlinked motor keeps 0.74 of its speed after one simulated second. Under load, a lower throttle mainly lowers the step and with it the draw. With infinite_batteries on, the draw helper supplies every request and takes no charge. An EMP pulse cuts the motor's supply while its countdown is 300 or more; supply then returns linearly over the next 300 updates, 5 simulated seconds.

families.summary: Small, medium and large tanks have 31.25, 187.5 and 703.125 L compartments that exchange with each port's pipe network; liquid pressure stays low until the last 80 L of room fills; contents drift toward ambient temperature with a time constant of 16.7 simulated seconds.

sections.title: Operating conditions
sections.body: The tank keeps its own compartment of volume 1.5625 × listed voxels: 3.125, 18.75 and 70.3125 units, 31.25, 187.5 and 703.125 L. Each Stored Fluid port stays on its own pipe network, and the tank exchanges each network with its compartment at bias 0 and factor 1. Tank Content reads 10 × the stored amount, in litres, and Tank Pressure reads atmospheres. Fluid tanks run water component case 8 and drift toward the surrounding temperature by 0.001 per update.

sections.title: Pressure and fill
sections.body: Pressure follows the compartment law, not the fill fraction. The medium and large tanks are above volume 8, so pure liquid in them reads under 0.5 atm until less than 80 L of room is left, then 7.5 atm more per 75 L, 60 when full. The small tank (volume 3.125) reads 60 × amount ÷ 3.125. Gas in the tank counts toward the same pressure.

sections.title: Initial contents
sections.body: A new tank component starts with fluid index 1, diesel, and fill 1. For a liquid other than diesel or jet fuel, the first build adds 0.99 × fill × V of it plus V ÷ 60 of air, split into nitrogen, oxygen and CO2. Inference from the decoded equations: before any exchange that reads about 60.4, 60.9 and 63.5 atm for the three sizes, because the air takes the last 1 % of room. Set to a gas, a fluid tank receives only 0.99 × fill × V ÷ 60 of it, 0.99 atm at full fill.

findings.label: Compartment pressure law
findings.detail: All 13 fluid indices (0 to 12) enter only as liquid sum L or gas sum G, with A = L + G. Pure gas reduces to P = 60 × A ÷ V at any volume. Pure liquid in a volume up to 8 (80 L), such as a pipe network of 4, also gives 60 × A ÷ V. Pure liquid above volume 8 gives max(0.5 × A ÷ V, 7.5 × (A − V + 8)): under 0.5 atm until less than 8 (80 L) of room is left, then 7.5 atm per amount (per 75 L) up to 60 at full. Temperature does not enter. Inference from the instruction sequence; degenerate states follow the original SSE arithmetic. Report: investigation/fluids-network.md.
